Unit K7.580-581 (K. VII 580–581). ENGLISH:
The pulses in the eight dyscrasias will have that form which we set out in the treatise on pulses. Whether, as has been said, it belongs to the blood alone, or arises from some admixture of a humour, one must determine by the accompanying colour of the whole body and by the other symptoms (those concerning sleep and waking, or appetite and lack of appetite, or anything of that kind, which were stated a little earlier), and by the preceding regimen, and the exercises, and the things that are accustomed to befall the patient himself, and further by the season and the country and the natural density and rarity of the body. For it is better to take the assurance for the diagnosis from all of these, not from one or two, knowing well that this alone in the art has the largest share in conjecture: I mean this whole diagnostic part of the art, not only that which concerns cacochymia or plethora, which we now propose to distinguish. For matters concerning the functions, or the causes of diseases, or the cures, admit of a more scientific knowledge. More has been said about these very matters elsewhere, and for now it will suffice, once we have adequately determined what has been added, to bring the writing to a close somewhere about here. The account would become adequate if it were examined by way of an example. Let it be, then, that the man is without fever, but that his veins are of greater bulk and his whole body redder.

Unit K7.581-582 (K. VII 581–582). ENGLISH:
One must therefore consider whether any of the heating causes has come near him; for if one should appear to have done so, it is better to postpone the diagnosis until the motion arising from it has settled down in the whole body, since it is not proper to bring to diagnosis someone who is angry, or has bathed, or is bathing, or has exercised, or has just taken wine, or has been heated in any other way whatsoever, but rather one who is at rest from all external motions. For if at that time he should appear such, blood is in excess in the person. From there one should examine the other signs, first those that have the greatest force, then the rest in order. It was shown that these are heaviness and tension, and reluctance towards movements, and then next the features of the pulses, sleeplessness and sleep, appetites and lack of appetite, and whatever other things are of this kind. After these, each of the antecedent factors that produce plethora: whether some habitual excretion has been suppressed, whether exercise has been neglected, whether larger quantities of highly nourishing foods have been taken continually, whether he makes use of unaccustomed baths after food, and in addition to these, whether such a person is frequently seized by plethoric diseases.

Unit K7.582-583 (K. VII 582–583). ENGLISH:
On top of all these, one adds also the indications from the region and the season, or anything else of this kind, without assigning equal importance to all of them, just as one does not in the other parts of the art either. For some of the signs are scientific, such as the tension, the heaviness, the swelling of the veins, the reluctance [to move], the colour, and the movement of the pulses, provided, obviously, that all recent motions have been excluded. Others fall short of these, such as the retention of the excretions, the idle life, foods that are more abundant and nourishing, and baths after food; yet all of them together come close to the scientific ones. Third in rank after these is whether the person is habitually seized by plethoric diseases. Next come the things belonging to regions and seasons that contribute to the formation of all of them. For in winter and spring, and in cold and temperate regions, people accumulate plethora more; in hot and dry seasons and regions, less. So too those who are dense at the surface accumulate it more, and those who are rarefied more rarely.
